g.q: We ___ a lovely time at my cousin's wedding last summer.
g.e: 'Have' + experience (have a good time) is lexical have. 'Have got' is only for possession and isn't used in the past simple.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I'm having got two older brothers.
g.e: 'Have' for possession or relationships is a state verb, so we don't use it in the continuous.

g.q: ___ your brother ever had his hair dyed?
g.e: Present perfect with 'ever': has + past participle. Here 'had' is the past participle of lexical have (have something done).

g.q: My parents ___ the kitchen repainted next week.
g.e: Have something done = someone else does it for you. Present continuous shows a future arrangement: are having it repainted.

g.q: I ___ (not / have) a chance to call my grandmother yet.
g.e: Present perfect with 'yet'. The auxiliary is have + not, and the main verb 'have' (have a chance) becomes 'had'.

g.q: You ___ (not / have to) come to the family reunion if you don't want to.
g.e: 'Have to' behaves like a normal verb, so the negative uses do/don't: you don't have to = it isn't necessary.

v.q: My sister never gives up, even when things get really difficult. She's very ___.
v.e: Determined people keep trying until they achieve what they want.

v.q: Someone who is ___ thinks they are better and more important than other people.
v.e: Arrogant = behaving as if you are better or more important than others.

v.q: My uncle is so ___ – he'll always tell you exactly what he thinks, even if it hurts.
v.e: Outspoken people say what they think directly, even if it upsets others.

v.q: A ___ person believes almost anything people tell them.
v.e: Gullible = too trusting, easily tricked into believing things.

v.q: My brother's mood changes very quickly and without warning. He's very m___.
v.e: Moody people change their mood suddenly, often becoming unhappy or bad-tempered.

v.q: Someone who does things carefully and always wants to do their work well is c___.
v.e: Conscientious = careful and hard-working, taking your duties seriously.

s: My grandfather has had the same barber in Bagheria since he was a young man.
We're having a big family lunch on Sunday, so I don't have time to study.
My older sister is incredibly determined, but she can be quite stubborn too.
Have you ever had your photo taken by a professional photographer?

g.q: ___ the long hours, she really enjoys working as a nurse.
g.e: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form. 'Although' and 'even though' need a full clause (subject + verb).

g.q: He took a part-time job ___ he could save up for university.
g.e: 'So that' + subject + verb (often with can/could) expresses purpose. 'In order to' and 'so as to' need an infinitive.

g.q: The factory closed ___ a fall in demand.
g.e: 'Owing to' (like 'due to') is followed by a noun. 'Because' and 'since' need a clause.

g.q: The salary was quite low. ___, she accepted the job because it was close to home.
g.e: 'Nevertheless' links two sentences to show contrast and is followed by a comma. 'Although' and 'despite' join ideas within one sentence.

g.q: I set two alarms so ___ not to be late for the interview.
g.e: 'So as not to' + infinitive expresses a negative purpose: I did it so as not to be late.

g.q: She was promoted in spite ___ having very little experience.
g.e: 'In spite of' always needs 'of', followed by a noun or -ing form.

v.q: If you are ___, you lose your job because the company no longer needs you, not because you did something wrong.
v.e: Made redundant = lose your job because it's no longer needed. Sacked = dismissed for doing something wrong.

v.q: She decided to ___ because she'd been offered a better job elsewhere.
v.e: Resign = leave your job by choice. 'Lay off' needs an object and 'apply' needs 'for'.

v.q: A ___ job is one where you work only for a fixed period, for example six months.
v.e: A temporary job lasts for a limited time. A permanent job has no end date.

v.q: Nurses often work ___: sometimes mornings, sometimes afternoons and sometimes nights.
v.e: Work shifts = work at different times of day in rotation with other workers.

v.q: Working extra hours after your normal working day is called working o___.
v.e: Overtime = time worked beyond your normal hours, often paid at a higher rate.

v.q: The extra things you get from a job apart from your salary, like a company car, are called p___.
v.e: Perks are extra benefits that come with a job, e.g. a company phone or free lunches.

s: Although the salary wasn't great, she accepted the job because of the flexible hours.
He was made redundant last year; however, he soon found a much better position.
I left early so as not to get stuck in the traffic on the way to Palermo.
Owing to the heavy rain, the meeting was postponed until next week.

g.q: When I was little, my grandmother ___ me stories every night before bed.
g.e: 'Would' + infinitive describes repeated actions or habits in the past, like 'used to'.

g.q: We ___ a dog called Rocky when I was a child.
g.e: Use 'used to', not 'would', for past states such as possession. 'Would' is only for repeated actions.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: When I was a child, I would live in a small flat near the sea.
When I was a child, I used to live in a small flat near the sea.
When I was a child, I was used to live in a small flat near the sea.
g.e: 'Live' here is a state, so we use 'used to', not 'would'. 'Be used to' means 'be accustomed to' and takes -ing.

g.q: I ___ along the beach when I suddenly saw a dolphin.
g.e: Past continuous gives the background to a specific incident, which is in the past simple (saw).

g.q: By the time we got to the station, the train ___ (already / leave).
g.e: Past perfect shows an action that happened before another past event: it had left before we arrived.

g.q: I ___ (not / use to) like vegetables, but now I love them.
g.e: After 'did/didn't' we use the base form 'use to', not 'used to'.

v.q: She has very happy memories of her ___.
v.e: The suffix -hood forms abstract nouns for periods of life or states: childhood, adulthood, parenthood.

v.q: Their ___ has lasted since primary school.
v.e: The suffix -ship forms nouns for relationships: friendship, relationship, partnership.

v.q: After years of living with her parents, she finally had her ___.
v.e: The suffix -dom forms abstract nouns from some adjectives: free → freedom, bored → boredom, wise → wisdom.

v.q: Many teenagers complain about ___ during the long summer holidays.
v.e: Bored → boredom, with the suffix -dom, like freedom.

v.q: He showed great ___ (kind) to the new students.
v.e: Add -ness to many adjectives to make abstract nouns: kind → kindness, happy → happiness.

v.q: Losing my wallet on the bus was a real ___ (embarrass).
v.e: Add -ment to some verbs to make nouns: embarrass → embarrassment, enjoy → enjoyment.

s: When we were kids, we would spend every summer at our grandparents' house by the sea.
I didn't use to like reading, but now I can't put a good book down.
My happiest memories of childhood are of playing football in the street with my neighbours.
I had just fallen asleep when the phone rang in the middle of the night.

g.q: My brother and I haven't spoken to ___ since the argument.
g.e: 'Each other' shows a two-way action between people. Reflexive pronouns (ourselves) mean the action returns to the same person.

g.q: ___ say that learning a language as a child is easier.
g.e: 'They' can mean people in general or experts: they say… 'One' would need 'says'.

g.q: ___ was a lot of noise coming from the classroom next door.
g.e: Use 'there' + be to say that something exists or is present: there was a lot of noise.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Did you enjoy at the party?
Did you enjoy you at the party?
Did you enjoy yourself at the party?
g.e: 'Enjoy' needs an object. If there's no other object, use a reflexive pronoun: enjoy yourself.

g.q: Nobody can do it for you; you have to do it ___ (you).
g.e: Reflexive pronouns can emphasise that someone does something without help: do it yourself.

g.q: The children made the cake all by ___.
g.e: 'By + reflexive pronoun' means alone or without help: all by themselves.

v.q: Words used by a particular group, such as doctors or IT workers, which other people may not understand, are called ___.
v.e: Jargon = specialist words used by a profession or group.

v.q: A ___ is a form of a language spoken in a particular region, with some of its own words and grammar.
v.e: A dialect has its own vocabulary and grammar, like Sicilian. An accent is only about pronunciation.

v.q: A person who has spoken two languages perfectly since childhood is ___.
v.e: Bi- means two: a bilingual person speaks two languages like a native.

v.q: 'Break a leg', meaning 'good luck', is an example of ___.
v.e: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is different from the meanings of the individual words.

v.q: Very informal words like 'cool' or 'mate' are called s___.
v.e: Slang = very informal words, often used by young people or particular groups.

v.q: When you know a word but can't quite remember it, it's on the t___ of your tongue.
v.e: 'On the tip of your tongue' = almost remembered but not quite.

s: They say that the best way to learn a language is to live in the country.
My cousin and I text each other in Sicilian dialect, which confuses everyone else.
Doctors often use so much jargon that their patients can't understand them.
Did you teach yourself Spanish, or did you take lessons at a school?

g.q: My bike ___ stolen outside the station last week.
g.e: 'Get' + past participle can replace 'be' in the passive, especially for unexpected events: it got stolen.

g.q: I finally ___ my brother to help me with my project.
g.e: Get someone to do something = persuade them. 'Make', 'have' and 'let' are followed by the infinitive without 'to'.

g.q: We need to ___ the washing machine repaired.
g.e: Get something done = arrange for someone else to do it, like 'have something done'.

g.q: It took me months to get used to ___ on the left in London.
g.e: In 'get used to', 'to' is a preposition, so it's followed by the -ing form.

g.q: They ___ (get / marry) in Cefalù last June.
g.e: 'Get' + adjective or past participle describes a change of state: get married, get lost, get tired.

g.q: Hurry up and ___ (get / dress), or we'll be late!
g.e: Get dressed = put your clothes on. 'Get' + past participle for actions we do to ourselves.

v.q: I don't really ___ my new flatmate; we argue about everything.
v.e: Get on with someone = have a good relationship with them.

v.q: It took her months to ___ the flu.
v.e: Get over an illness or a problem = recover from it.

v.q: I keep meaning to reply to your email, but I never ___ it.
v.e: Get round to doing something = finally find time to do it.

v.q: What are you ___? Just tell me what you mean!
v.e: What are you getting at? = What are you trying to suggest?

v.q: He copied his friend's homework and the teacher didn't notice, so he got a___ with it.
v.e: Get away with something = do something wrong and not be punished.

v.q: I don't earn much, but I can get b___ on my salary.
v.e: Get by = manage to live with the money or things you have.

s: I'm getting my hair cut on Saturday, so I can't come to the beach.
It took me ages to get used to getting up so early for work.
My parents got married in a little church near Bagheria.
Don't worry, you'll soon get over it and feel much better.

g.q: I don't mind lending you the money. ___, you're my best friend.
g.e: 'After all' introduces a reason that supports what you've just said.

g.q: We'd better leave now; ___, we'll miss the last bus.
g.e: 'Otherwise' means 'if not': if we don't leave now, we'll miss the bus.

g.q: The weather was awful, but ___ we didn't get lost.
g.e: 'At least' introduces a positive point in a negative situation.

g.q: ___, did you hear that Marco is moving to Milan?
g.e: 'By the way' introduces a new topic or something you've just remembered.

g.q: I didn't think I'd like the film. In f___, it was brilliant.
g.e: 'In fact' (like 'actually') introduces surprising or contrasting information.

g.q: There were a few problems, but ___ in all, it was a great holiday.
g.e: 'All in all' introduces a general conclusion after considering everything.

v.q: An agreement to stop fighting for a period of time is a ___.
v.e: A ceasefire is an agreement to stop fighting, often temporarily.

v.q: People who are forced to leave their country because of war are ___.
v.e: Refugees escape from war or danger to another country.

v.q: When an army moves back and away from the enemy because it is losing, it ___.
v.e: Retreat = move away from the enemy. Surrender = officially stop fighting and accept defeat.

v.q: A war between groups of people from the same country is a ___ war.
v.e: A civil war is fought between groups within one country.

v.q: The people killed or injured in a war or accident are called c___.
v.e: Casualties = people who are killed or injured.

v.q: Countries that fight on the same side in a war are a___.
v.e: Allies are countries that support each other, especially in a war.

s: Basically, the film is about two brothers who end up fighting on opposite sides of a civil war.
I know it's expensive, but after all, it's your birthday and you deserve a treat.
Both sides finally agreed to a ceasefire after months of peace talks.
We'd better book the tickets now; otherwise, they'll all be sold out.

g.q: Never ___ such a moving ending to a novel.
g.e: After a negative adverb like 'never' at the start, we invert the subject and auxiliary: never have I read.

g.q: No sooner had the film started ___ the power went off.
g.e: 'No sooner… than' is a fixed pair. 'Hardly… when' is the other common pattern.

g.q: Hardly ___ the book down when my phone rang.
g.e: 'Hardly' at the start needs inversion with the past perfect: hardly had I… when…

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Little I knew that the author was my neighbour.
Little did I know that the author was my neighbour.
Little knew I that the author was my neighbour.
Little I did know that the author was my neighbour.
g.e: 'Little' at the start (= not at all) needs inversion. In the past simple we add 'did': little did I know.

g.q: Not only ___ (she / write) the script, but she also directed the film.
g.e: After 'not only' at the start we invert, adding 'did' in the past simple: not only did she write…

g.q: Only when I finished the book ___ (I / understand) the title.
g.e: With 'only when' at the start, the inversion happens in the main clause: only when… did I understand.

v.q: A film with an exciting story that holds your attention completely is ___.
v.e: Gripping = so exciting that you can't stop watching or reading.

v.q: The plot was completely ___; nothing like that could ever happen in real life.
v.e: Far-fetched = very difficult to believe.

v.q: The film is ___ a true story about a Sicilian fisherman.
v.e: 'Based on' tells us where the story comes from: based on a true story or a novel.

v.q: I cried at the end; it was really ___.
v.e: Moving = making you feel strong emotions, especially sadness.

v.q: The book was so good that I couldn't put it d___.
v.e: 'I couldn't put it down' = the book was so interesting that I didn't want to stop reading.

v.q: A film or book that makes you think seriously about things is t___-provoking.
v.e: Thought-provoking = making people think carefully about an issue.

s: Never have I read such a gripping novel; I finished it in one night.
Not only was the plot predictable, but the acting was also terrible.
Little did we know that the film was based on a true story.
The film is set in Palermo and the soundtrack is absolutely stunning.

g.q: She ___ be at home; her car isn't outside.
g.e: 'Can't' shows you are sure something is NOT true. 'Mustn't' means it's prohibited, not a deduction.

g.q: I can hear someone singing next door. It ___ be the new neighbour.
g.e: 'Must' shows you are almost sure something is true, based on evidence.

g.q: It's highly ___ that they'll cancel the concert.
g.e: 'It's (highly) likely that…' shows something will probably happen. We can't say 'It's highly sure/bound'.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: They might forgotten about the meeting.
They might have forget about the meeting.
They might had forgotten about the meeting.
They might have forgotten about the meeting.
g.e: For speculation about the past, use modal + have + past participle: might have forgotten.

g.q: You ___ (must / hear) the thunder last night; it was so loud!
g.e: Must have + past participle = you're sure something happened in the past.

g.q: She ___ (can't / see) us; she walked straight past.
g.e: Can't/couldn't have + past participle = you're sure something didn't happen.

v.q: The door ___ as it opened slowly in the dark.
v.e: Creak = make a long high sound, like an old door or wooden floor.

v.q: Please don't ___; nobody can understand what you're saying.
v.e: Mumble = speak quietly and unclearly, so it's hard to understand.

v.q: She ___ when she saw the huge spider on her pillow.
v.e: Scream = make a loud, high cry because you are frightened.

v.q: He let out a long ___ of relief when he heard his exam results.
v.e: A sigh is a long breath out, showing relief, tiredness or sadness.

v.q: To speak very quietly so that only one person can hear you is to w___.
v.e: Whisper = speak very softly, using your breath rather than your voice.

v.q: The sound of dry leaves or paper moving is a r___.
v.e: Rustle = the soft sound of dry leaves or paper moving.

s: Someone must have left the window open, because I can hear the traffic outside.
She can't have heard you, as she was wearing her headphones.
The floorboards creaked and somebody whispered my name in the dark.
They're bound to be tired after such a long journey from Palermo.

g.q: The new shopping centre ___ to be opening next spring.
g.e: Be said/thought/believed + to + infinitive distances the speaker from the information: people say it.

g.q: There ___ to be a problem with your booking.
g.e: 'There seems to be' is a polite, less direct way of saying there is a problem.

g.q: The thieves are believed ___ through a back window.
g.e: Use the perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) when the belief is about a past event.

g.q: It ___ that the company will lose hundreds of jobs.
g.e: It + passive reporting verb + that: it is feared/thought/said that… The speaker isn't saying it's certain.

g.q: The singer is thought ___ (be) living in London at the moment.
g.e: Be thought + to be + -ing for a continuous situation now.

g.q: A___ to the weather forecast, it's going to rain tomorrow.
g.e: 'According to' shows that information comes from someone else, not from you.

v.q: I'm not in a hurry. Take your ___.
v.e: Take your time = don't hurry.

v.q: We got to the station just ___ time to catch the train.
v.e: In time = early enough. On time = at the planned time.

v.q: The concert started ___ time, at exactly eight o'clock.
v.e: On time = punctually, at the planned time.

v.q: Since I retired, I've got a lot of time on my ___.
v.e: Have time on your hands = have a lot of free time and not much to do.

v.q: There's no hurry. We've got plenty of time to s___.
v.e: Time to spare = more time than you need.

v.q: Playing video games all day is a complete w___ of time.
v.e: A waste of time = a useless way to spend time.

s: Apparently, the new restaurant in the square is going to open next month.
The museum is said to be one of the most interesting in Sicily.
There seems to have been a mistake with our booking, I'm afraid.
Don't rush; take your time and make sure you check everything carefully.

g.q: I wish I ___ more money so I could travel.
g.e: Wish + past simple for things we'd like to be different now.

g.q: It's time we ___ saving for the holiday.
g.e: It's (high) time + past simple, even though we are talking about now or the future.

g.q: I'd rather you ___ my credit card without asking.
g.e: Would rather + another person + past simple: I'd rather you didn't…

g.q: If only I ___ that expensive phone last month!
g.e: If only + past perfect expresses regret about the past.

g.q: He spends money as if he ___ (be) a millionaire.
g.e: As if + past tense for unreal situations. 'Were' is more formal; 'was' is common in speech.

g.q: I wish my parents ___ (lend) me the money last year, but they refused.
g.e: Wish + past perfect to talk about a past situation we regret.

v.q: She's always ___; she can never afford anything by the end of the month.
v.e: Broke (informal) = having no money.

v.q: Our neighbours are really ___; they've got three houses and a boat.
v.e: Well off = rich. Hard up = short of money.

v.q: The flat was a real ___; we paid much less than we expected.
v.e: A bargain is something that costs less than its real value. A rip-off costs too much.

v.q: A loan from a bank to buy a house is a ___.
v.e: A mortgage is a long-term loan to buy property.

v.q: Someone who hates spending money is t___-fisted.
v.e: Tight-fisted (informal) = not willing to spend money.

v.q: Charities are organisations that are not for p___.
v.e: Not-for-profit organisations use their money to help people, not to make owners rich.

s: I wish I had saved more money when I was younger.
It's high time we opened a savings account for our summer holiday.
If only we hadn't taken out such a big mortgage on the flat!
I'd rather you didn't lend him any more money, because he never pays it back.

g.q: My parents never let me ___ out late.
g.e: Let + object + infinitive without 'to': let me stay.

g.q: I don't mind people ___ in the library as long as they're quiet.
g.e: Mind + object + -ing: I don't mind people eating.

g.q: The doctor advised him ___ more exercise.
g.e: Advise + object + to + infinitive: advise someone to do something.

g.q: The teacher made us ___ the whole essay again.
g.e: Make + object + infinitive without 'to': make us rewrite.

g.q: Can you remind me ___ (call) the dentist tomorrow?
g.e: Remind + object + to + infinitive.

g.q: I'd like you ___ (help) me move the sofa.
g.e: Would like + object + to + infinitive.

v.q: He's so ___; he forgets everything and he's lost his keys twice today.
v.e: Absent-minded = often forgetting things because you're thinking about something else.

v.q: My grandmother is very ___; she'll listen to anyone's point of view.
v.e: Open-minded = willing to accept different ideas and opinions.

v.q: Someone who says nice things to your face but criticises you behind your back is ___.
v.e: Two-faced = not sincere; saying different things to different people.

v.q: Our volunteers are all very ___ and are always willing to help others.
v.e: Kind-hearted = kind and generous to others.

v.q: Someone who thinks they are better or cleverer than everyone else is b___-headed.
v.e: Big-headed = too proud of yourself.

v.q: Someone who is relaxed and doesn't get upset or worried easily is easy-g___.
v.e: Easy-going = calm and relaxed.

s: My parents always encouraged me to volunteer at the local animal shelter.
I can't stand people telling me what to do when I'm only trying to help.
Volunteering has made me much more open-minded and patient with people.
The coach made us run round the pitch before every training session.

g.q: If I ___ my phone charger, I'd be able to call you now.
g.e: Mixed conditional: if + past perfect (past cause), would + infinitive (present result).

g.q: ___ you need any help, just send me a message.
g.e: 'Should you need' = 'if you need'. It's a formal way of starting a conditional.

g.q: You can borrow my laptop ___ you're careful with it.
g.e: 'As long as' = only if: this is the condition.

g.q: ___ I known about the problem, I would have fixed it.
g.e: 'Had I known' = 'if I had known'. Inversion replaces 'if' in formal third conditionals.

g.q: I'll go to the beach tomorrow u___ it rains.
g.e: 'Unless' = if… not: I'll go if it doesn't rain.

g.q: If she ___ (not / stay) up all night on her phone, she wouldn't be so tired now.
g.e: Mixed conditional: past perfect for the past condition, would + infinitive for the present result.

v.q: I'm completely addicted ___ my phone.
v.e: Addicted to something.

v.q: My brother is obsessed ___ video games.
v.e: Obsessed with something.

v.q: Don't forget to ___ your files before you update the software.
v.e: Back up = make a copy of your files in case the original is lost.

v.q: The app keeps ___, so I have to restart it.
v.e: When an app or computer crashes, it suddenly stops working.

v.q: I'm not very keen ___ social media.
v.e: Keen on something = interested in it or liking it.

v.q: She's really good ___ fixing computers.
v.e: Good at something/doing something.

s: If I hadn't dropped my phone in the sea, I wouldn't need a new one now.
You can use my laptop as long as you back up your files first.
Should the app crash again, please contact our technical support team.
My little brother is completely addicted to his tablet and never looks up.

g.q: You ___ have brought any food; there's plenty here.
g.e: Needn't have + past participle = you did it, but it wasn't necessary.

g.q: We ___ wear our uniform on the school trip, but most of us did anyway.
g.e: Didn't have to = it wasn't necessary (in the past). 'Needn't' alone refers to the present.

g.q: Visitors ___ to take photos inside the museum.
g.e: Be allowed to = have permission. 'Mustn't' and 'can't' are followed by the infinitive without 'to'.

g.q: Which sentence means 'I did it, but it wasn't necessary'?
o: I didn't need to take a taxi.
I needn't have taken a taxi.
I mustn't have taken a taxi.
I didn't have to take a taxi.
g.e: Needn't have + past participle means you did something unnecessary. 'Didn't need to' usually means you didn't do it.

g.q: We're s___ to be there by eight, but we'll probably be late.
g.e: Be supposed to = be expected to, often when it doesn't happen.

g.q: You'd ___ (better / not) tell anyone about this.
g.e: Had better (not) + infinitive for strong advice. The negative is 'had better not', not 'hadn't better'.

v.q: I think you've ___ what I said; that's not what I meant.
v.e: The prefix mis- means 'wrongly': misunderstand, mispronounce, misspell.

v.q: The meat was dry because I ___ it.
v.e: Over- means 'too much': overcook, oversleep, overcharge.

v.q: Our team was completely ___ by a much stronger side.
v.e: Out- means 'better or more than': outplay, outnumber, outlive.

v.q: She's very ___-government and supports all its policies.
v.e: Pro- means 'in favour of'. Anti- means 'against'.

v.q: I can't find my keys; I've m___ them again.
v.e: Misplace (or mislay) = put something somewhere and then be unable to find it. Mis- means wrongly.

v.q: They paid him too little for all his work; he was ___ (pay).
v.e: Under- means 'too little': underpaid, underestimate, undercooked.

s: You needn't have bought so much food; there's enough for the whole week.
Students aren't allowed to use their phones during lessons unless the teacher says so.
We were supposed to meet at the station, but I misunderstood the time.
You'd better not overcook the pasta, or my grandmother will be furious.

g.q: This soup tastes ___.
g.e: Sense verbs (taste, look, sound, smell, feel) are followed by adjectives, not adverbs.

g.q: You look ___ you haven't slept for days.
g.e: Look/seem/sound + as if (or like) + clause.

g.q: I heard someone ___ the piano as I walked past the gallery.
g.e: Hear/see + object + -ing for an action in progress.

g.q: This painting looks ___ a photograph.
g.e: Look like + noun: it looks like a photograph.

g.q: I saw him ___ (walk) out of the museum without paying.
g.e: See + object + infinitive (the whole action) or -ing (part of it in progress). Both are correct here.

g.q: Your idea sounds really ___ (interest).
g.e: Sound + adjective: it sounds interesting.

v.q: When he said that, I really saw ___. I was furious.
v.e: See red = become very angry.

v.q: Suddenly, out of the ___, my cousin from Australia called me.
v.e: Out of the blue = completely unexpectedly.

v.q: She was ___ with envy when she saw my new bike.
v.e: Green with envy = very jealous.

v.q: A painting of a person is a ___.
v.e: A portrait shows a person. A landscape shows countryside.

v.q: A painting of fruit, flowers or objects on a table is a still l___.
v.e: A still life shows objects that don't move.

v.q: A place where you can see and sometimes buy works of art is a g___.
v.e: Art gallery = a room or building for showing art.

s: This painting looks as if it was painted by a child, but it's worth a fortune.
I could hear the waves crashing on the rocks from my bedroom window.
When I saw the price of the ticket, I went as white as a sheet.
Out of the blue, my teacher asked me to paint a portrait of my grandmother.

g.q: I hate ___ told what to do.
g.e: Passive gerund: being + past participle. I hate it when people tell me what to do.

g.q: She denied ___ the medicine without a prescription.
g.e: Deny + -ing. The perfect gerund (having + past participle) stresses that the action was in the past.

g.q: He seems ___ a lot of weight since the operation.
g.e: Seem + perfect infinitive (to have + past participle) for something that happened before now.

g.q: There's no point ___ antibiotics for a cold.
g.e: There's no point in + -ing = it's useless to do it.

g.q: It's not worth ___ (see) a doctor for such a small cut.
g.e: It's (not) worth + -ing.

g.q: The patient was lucky ___ (survive) the accident.
g.e: Adjective + to-infinitive. The perfect infinitive stresses the past, but the simple infinitive is also correct.

v.q: She was so nervous she was shaking like a ___.
v.e: Shake like a leaf = shake a lot because you're frightened or nervous.

v.q: I slept like a ___ last night and feel great today.
v.e: Sleep like a log = sleep very deeply.

v.q: A doctor who performs operations is a ___.
v.e: A surgeon operates on patients. A GP is a family doctor.

v.q: My grandfather has to take ___ every day for his blood pressure.
v.e: Medication = medicine you take regularly. A prescription is the doctor's written order for it.

v.q: An unwanted extra effect of a medicine, for example feeling sleepy, is a s___ effect.
v.e: Side effects are unwanted results of taking a medicine.

v.q: After the holiday I felt as fit as a f___.
v.e: As fit as a fiddle = very healthy.

s: I hate being given injections, but I know it's worth having the flu vaccine.
He seems to have made a full recovery after his operation last month.
My grandfather sleeps like a log after a long walk along the seafront.
There's no point in taking antibiotics if you've just got a cold.

g.q: Hurry up! The train is ___ to leave.
g.e: Be about to + infinitive = going to happen very soon. 'On the point' needs 'of + -ing'.

g.q: The President ___ visit Palermo next month.
g.e: Be to + infinitive is used for formal, official arrangements.

g.q: This time tomorrow, we ___ on the beach in Mondello.
g.e: Future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action in progress at a particular future time.

g.q: The new airport terminal is ___ to open in May.
g.e: Be due to + infinitive = scheduled to happen at a particular time.

g.q: By the time you arrive, we ___ (finish) dinner.
g.e: Future perfect (will have + past participle) for an action completed before a future time.

g.q: I'm on the ___ of booking a trip to London.
g.e: Be on the point/verge of + -ing = be just about to do something.

v.q: The hotel was in the middle of nowhere; it was really ___.
v.e: Off the beaten track = far from where most tourists go.

v.q: The beach was so ___ that we couldn't find anywhere to put our towels.
v.e: Overcrowded = with too many people.

v.q: Mondello is ___ with tourists in August.
v.e: Packed with = very full of people.

v.q: A place that has not been changed or damaged by tourism is ___.
v.e: Unspoilt = still natural and beautiful, not damaged by development.

v.q: We went on a guided t___ of the old town.
v.e: A guided tour is a visit with a guide who explains things.

v.q: The view from the top of the mountain was b___; it was so beautiful.
v.e: Breathtaking = extremely beautiful or impressive.

s: We're about to set off on a road trip round the west of Sicily.
By this time next week, I'll be lying on an unspoilt beach far from the crowds.
The new museum is due to open in the spring, so book your tickets early.
I'd love to explore somewhere that's off the beaten track and not too touristy.

g.q: 'Would you like to come to the zoo with us?' 'I'd love ___!'
g.e: We can leave out the verb after 'to' if it's clear: I'd love to (come).

g.q: 'Will the shops be closed on Sunday?' 'I don't think ___.'
g.e: 'So' replaces a whole clause after think, hope, expect: I don't think so.

g.q: 'I've never had a pet.' '___ I.'
g.e: Neither + auxiliary + subject agrees with a negative statement. The auxiliary matches the tense: have.

g.q: My sister hates spiders, but I ___.
g.e: We use the auxiliary alone to avoid repeating the verb: but I don't (hate spiders).

g.q: I didn't want to feed the neighbour's cat, but I had ___.
g.e: After 'have to', 'want to', etc., we can keep only 'to' and leave out the verb.

g.q: 'Does your dog bite?' 'No, he ___.'
g.e: Short answers repeat the auxiliary, not the main verb.

v.q: A dog with no home that lives on the streets is a ___ dog.
v.e: A stray animal has no owner or home.

v.q: An animal species with very few individuals left is ___.
v.e: Endangered = in danger of disappearing. Extinct = no longer exists.

v.q: Animals kept in zoos live in ___.
v.e: In captivity = kept in a zoo or cage, not free.

v.q: Which is a group of sheep?
v.e: A flock of sheep or birds. A herd of cows, a swarm of bees, a pack of wolves.

v.q: A doctor for animals is a v___.
v.e: Vet (veterinary surgeon) = an animal doctor.

v.q: The natural environment where an animal lives is its h___.
v.e: Habitat = the natural home of an animal or plant.

s: I'd love to adopt a stray dog, but my parents won't let me.
My brother doesn't like cats, but I do, so we're always arguing about pets.
Many species are endangered because they're losing their natural habitat.
I don't think so, but I'll ask the vet when we take the puppy in tomorrow.

g.q: I'm taking a ___ holiday in August.
g.e: Time expressions can use the possessive: a month's holiday, a week's rest.

g.q: My ___ lasagne is the best in Bagheria.
g.e: Possessive 's for people: my grandmother's lasagne.

g.q: After a ___ cooking course, I can finally make fresh pasta.
g.e: In compound adjectives with numbers, the noun is singular and hyphenated: a two-week course.

g.q: Could you get the ___ from the cupboard? I need to make a cake.
g.e: Compound noun for a container's purpose: a cake tin. 'A tin of cake' means a tin full of cake.

g.q: She's a friend of ___ (I).
g.e: A friend of + possessive pronoun: a friend of mine/yours/hers.

g.q: The ___ (children) bedroom is at the end of the corridor.
g.e: Irregular plurals not ending in s add 's: children's, women's, people's.

v.q: ___ the cheese and sprinkle it over the pasta.
v.e: Grate = rub food against a grater to make small pieces.

v.q: ___ the eggs and sugar together until light and fluffy.
v.e: Whisk = mix quickly to add air.

v.q: ___ the dough for ten minutes before letting it rise.
v.e: Knead = press and fold dough with your hands.

v.q: Food cooked in hot water vapour, not in the water itself, is ___.
v.e: Steamed food is cooked over boiling water, not in it.

v.q: S___ the sauce with a wooden spoon so it doesn't stick to the pan.
v.e: Stir = move a spoon round and round in a liquid.

v.q: Arancine are rice balls that are s___ with meat sauce or cheese and then fried.
v.e: Stuffed = filled with another food.

s: My grandmother's recipe for arancine is a closely guarded family secret.
First peel and chop the onions, then fry them gently in olive oil.
Could you put the chopping board back in the kitchen cupboard, please?
We're having a barbecue at my cousin's house by the sea this weekend.

g.q: The athlete, ___ coach is from Palermo, won a gold medal.
g.e: 'Whose' shows possession: the athlete's coach. 'Who's' = who is.

g.q: He missed the penalty, ___ really annoyed the fans.
g.e: 'Which' can refer to a whole clause. 'That' can't be used in non-defining clauses.

g.q: The players, most of ___ were very young, played brilliantly.
g.e: After quantifiers + of (most of, some of, all of) we use 'whom' for people.

g.q: This is the stadium ___ we watched the final.
g.e: 'Where' = in which. 'Which' or 'that' would need 'in' at the end.

g.q: The race, ___ I had been training for months, was cancelled.
g.e: In formal English the preposition goes before 'which': train for → for which.

g.q: My coach, to ___ I owe everything, retired last year.
g.e: After a preposition, use 'whom' for people.

v.q: The team's ___ was due to months of hard training.
v.e: After 'the team's' we need a noun: success.

v.q: She's very ___; she wants to be the best in the world.
v.e: After 'very' we need an adjective: ambitious.

v.q: We need to ___ the path so two people can walk side by side.
v.e: Some adjectives form verbs with -en: wide → widen, short → shorten.

v.q: The ___ of the pool is fifty metres.
v.e: Long → length (noun), lengthen (verb).

v.q: Regular exercise can ___ (strong) your muscles.
v.e: Strong → strength (noun) → strengthen (verb).

v.q: She showed great ___ (patient) during the long race.
v.e: Patient (adjective) → patience (noun).

s: The runner, whose training had been interrupted by injury, still managed to finish.
We lost the match, which was really disappointing for the whole team.
Regular training will strengthen your legs and improve your confidence.
My coach, to whom I owe a great deal, has just retired.

g.q: ___ I really need is a long holiday.
g.e: A cleft sentence with 'what' emphasises the thing: What I need is…

g.q: It was my sister ___ told me the news.
g.e: It + be + person + who emphasises the person.

g.q: All I want ___ a bit of peace and quiet.
g.e: 'All I want' is singular, so we use 'is'.

g.q: What happened ___ that we got completely lost.
g.e: What happened was (that)… is used to tell a story with emphasis.

g.q: The ___ why I left was that I felt homesick.
g.e: The reason why… is/was that… emphasises the reason.

g.q: W___ drives me crazy is people who never say thank you.
g.e: What + clause + is… emphasises the part after 'is'.

v.q: He's very ___; he cries at sad films.
v.e: Sensitive = easily upset. Sensible = practical and reasonable.

v.q: Our new car is very ___; it uses very little petrol.
v.e: Economical = not using much money or fuel. Economic = about the economy.

v.q: ___, I'm living with my parents, but I hope to move out soon.
v.e: Currently = now. Eventually = in the end. Recently and lately usually go with the present perfect, not the present continuous.

v.q: Could you ___ me your pen for a minute?
v.e: Lend = give temporarily. Borrow = take temporarily.

v.q: The price of petrol continues to r___.
v.e: Rise (no object) = go up. Raise needs an object: raise prices.

v.q: Too much screen time can a___ your sleep.
v.e: Affect is a verb. Effect is usually a noun.

s: What I really love about Bagheria is the view of the sea from the hills.
It was my grandfather who first taught me to swim in the sea.
The reason why I moved abroad was that I wanted to improve my English.
Could you lend me your dictionary, or should I borrow one from the library?
